article_text:
NAZA ナザ

劇場公開日： 2026年10月24日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

映画チケットを U-NEXTでお得にゲット PR

解説・あらすじ

「ノー・アザー・ランド 故郷は他にない」の監督を務めたイスラエル人ジャーナリストのユバル・アブラハームとラヘル・ショールが、パレスチナ・ガザ地区における民間人虐殺の真相に迫ったドキュメンタリー。 2023年10月7日のハマスによる襲撃をきっかけにイスラエル軍が開始したガザへの攻撃で、犠牲者は7万3000人以上にのぼるが、その大半は民間人だ。イスラエル軍は表向きには「民間人の犠牲は最小限に努めている」と主張するが、実際には民間人に被害が及ぶことを組織的に承認したうえで大規模攻撃を遂行していた。アブラハーム監督とショール監督は、夜のテルアビブのとある建物の屋上で、イスラエル軍の兵士や諜報員24人に極秘インタビューを実施し、ガザでの民間人殺害について「どのような指令を受けたのか」「何をしたのか」という証言を引き出していく。それぞれの言葉から浮かび上がったのは、イスラエル国家が組織的に作り上げた「虐殺を可能にするシステム」だった。 タイトルの「NAZA」は、イスラエル軍が標的であるハマス構成員を攻撃する際に、その巻き添えで犠牲になると予測される民間人の数を表す軍事用語。製作総指揮には「関心領域」のジョナサン・グレイザー監督が名を連ねた。2026年・第83回ベネチア国際映画祭コンペティション部門で審査員特別賞を受賞。

2026年製作／80分／G／イギリス・アメリカ合作 原題または英題：Naza 配給：トランスフォーマー 劇場公開日：2026年10月24日

オフィシャルサイト

スタッフ・キャスト

監督

ユバル・アブラハーム

ラヘル・ショール

製作総指揮

ジョナサン・グレイザー

article_text:
Artículos

Estrenos MUBI – 26 al 30 de octubre de 2026 y todo el mes

Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás este mes?

Para cinéfilos que busquen ampliar sus horizontes y descubrir ambiciosas películas de autores visionarios, desde realizadores emergentes hasta directores consagrados, existe MUBI. Con títulos exclusivos y una colección en constante rotación que son cuidadosamente seleccionadas por sus curadores. Conoce aquí todos los estrenos de películas y series que llegan este mes al catálogo de MUBI.

¿Cuánto cuesta la mensualidad de MUBI?

En México, la suscripción mensual cuesta $179 pesos , después del período de prueba de 7 días. O si lo prefieres, puedes ahorrar un 34% con la suscripción anual que asciende a $1,500 pesos.

Para estudiantes universitarios existe una opción especial para contratar y acceder a las películas de MUBI por solo $89 pesos al mes, tras una prueba gratuita de 30 días.

Aunque te puedes suscribir directamente en su plataforma, también lo puedes obtener de manera fácil a través de Prime Video .

También te podrían interesar los estrenos de:

NOTA: Los estrenos de esta semana están destacados en amarillo.

Estrenos de películas en MUBI (octubre 2026)

Toro salvaje (Raging Bull, Dir. Martin Scorsese, 1980) (23/10/2026)

Videodrome (Videodrome, Dir. David Cronenberg, 1983) (01/10/2026) El presidente de un canal de televisión de cable descubre una señal que transmite escenas de tortura y asesinato, y empieza a obsesionarse hasta el punto de no poder distinguir entre la realidad y las alucinaciones. Obra maestra del body horror que explora la violencia mediática, la tecnología y la carne como superficies intercambiables. Uno de los títulos fundamentales de Cronenberg y del cine canadiense.

Day of the Dead (Day of the Dead, Dir. George A. Romero, 1985) (01/10/2026) Tercera entrega de la saga de muertos vivientes de Romero. En un bunker subterráneo, un pequeño grupo de científicos y militares intenta sobrevivir mientras el mundo exterior ha sido ya devorado por los zombis. Un retrato de la desintegración del orden social y la razón humana más oscuro y pesimista que sus predecesores.

La cosa (The Thing, Dir. John Carpenter, 1982) (01/10/2026) Un grupo de investigadores en la Antártida descubre una forma de vida extraterrestre capaz de imitar a la perfección a cualquier ser vivo. El terror a lo desconocido y la paranoia de no saber quién entre los tuyos ya no es humano. Considerada una de las mejores películas de terror y ciencia ficción de la historia.

Arrebato (Arrebato, Dir. Iván Zulueta, 1980) (01/10/2026) Un director de cine de serie B recibe una cinta de súper 8 de un viejo conocido, Pedro, un joven fascinado por la magia del cine hasta niveles perturbadores. La película de culto del cine español por excelencia: un viaje hipnótico hacia la adicción, el éxtasis y la autodestrucción a través del acto de filmar. Restaurada y reivindicada como obra capital del cine europeo.

Adolescencia, sexo y muerte en Campamento Miasma (Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, Dir. Jane Schoenbrun, 2026) (02/10/2026) Tras años de secuelas cutres y un fandom en declive, la franquicia slasher Camp Miasma es puesta en manos de Vera, una joven directora obsesiva y apasionada que creció viendo la película original en secreto. Cuando visita a la actriz de la película original —una estrella reclusa envuelta en rumores— lo que comienza como una investigación se transforma en una relación cargada de tensión e intimidad inquietante. La cineasta no binaria Jane Schoenbrun ( I Saw the TV Glow ) estrena esta comedia slasher en Cannes 2026. Con Gillian Anderson y Hannah Einbinder.

Belle (Belle / バケモノの子, Dir. Mamoru Hosoda, 2021) (09/10/2026) Suzu es una adolescente tímida que encuentra refugio en el universo virtual de U, donde se convierte en Belle, una cantante con millones de seguidores. Cuando conoce a una bestia perseguida y temida por todos, emprende una búsqueda que la llevará a descubrir la verdad detrás de esa figura. Una reinvención del cuento de La Bella y la Bestia que exploró los fenómenos de identidad digital, el bullying y la soledad adolescente. Candidata de Japón a los Óscar 2022.

Fausto (Faust, Dir. F.W. Murnau, 1926) (14/10/2026) La cima del expresionismo alemán mudo. El viejo alquimista Fausto vende su alma al demonio Mefistófeles a cambio de la juventud eterna, desatando una cadena de tragedias. La película de Murnau es una de las obras visuales más impresionantes de la historia del cine, con efectos especiales pioneros y una fotografía que influyó en décadas de cine fantástico.

Principio y fin (Principio y fin, Dir. Arturo Ripstein, 1993) (16/10/2026) Adaptación de la novela del Premio Nobel Naguib Mahfouz, trasladada a la Ciudad de México. Tras la muerte del padre, una madre decide sacrificar el bienestar de sus cuatro hijos para costearle la carrera universitaria al menor, el favorito. Un retrato devastador de la pobreza, el sacrificio y la destrucción de una familia. Ganó el Ariel a Mejor Película en México.

Colección de cortometrajes de Mark Jenkin (16/10/2026) Una selección de cortometrajes del cineasta británico Mark Jenkin ( Bait , Enys Men , Rose of Nevada ), filmados en su totalidad en súper 8 y 16mm en las costas de Cornualles. Cada pieza es una exploración analógica de la memoria, la identidad y la relación entre las personas y los paisajes que habitan. Tomato (2017, 8 min.) — Retrato elegante de un artista; meditación lúdica sobre el paisaje, el color y el proceso colaborativo del cine. Vertical Shapes in a Horizontal Landscape (2018, 5 min.) — Una peregrinación a lo largo de la costa sur de Inglaterra hacia la casa de Derek Jarman en Dungeness. David Bowie is Dead (2018, 17 min.) — Un viaje de conciencia de flujo a través de Londres en el turbulento despertar de la muerte de David Bowie. I Saw the Face of God in the Jet Wash (2025, 17 min.) — Entre proyecciones alrededor del mundo, Jenkin reflexiona sobre influencias cinematográficas y la idea del hogar. Premio al Mejor Cortometraje Británico e Irlandés. Enough to Fill Up an Eggcup (2016, 36 min.) — Una parábola sobre el trabajo, la ecología y la humanidad, filmada en un pueblo pesquero de Cornualles. Cape Cornwall Calling / All the White Horses (2013, 6 min.) — Experimento según el manifiesto Silent Dancing Landscape Grain 13 de Jenkin.

Shot Reverse Shot (Shot Reverse Shot / Plan contraplan, Dir. Radu Jude y Adrian Cioflâncă, 2026) (23/10/2026) (Cortometraje, 22 min.) Entre 1985 y 1987, el periodista estadounidense Edward Serotta recorrió la Rumania comunista fotografiando la vida cotidiana bajo el régimen de Ceaușescu, en particular la comunidad judía. Lo que Serotta no sabía era que la Securitate, la policía secreta, lo seguía paso a paso y lo fotografiaba a él fotografiando. Cuarenta años después, Radu Jude y el historiador Adrian Cioflâncă reúnen los dos archivos en un plano-contraplano que revela la ironía cómica de la Historia. Presentado en la Berlinale 2026.

Toro salvaje (Raging Bull, Dir. Martin Scorsese, 1980) (23/10/2026) La vida del boxeador Jake LaMotta: su ascenso y caída dentro y fuera del ring, su brutalidad autodestructiva, sus celos enfermizos y su incapacidad para recibir el amor que su propia violencia aleja. Robert De Niro ganó el Óscar a Mejor Actor en uno de los papeles más físicos y perturbadores de la historia. Fotografiada en blanco y negro por Michael Chapman; considerada una de las grandes películas del cine americano.

El último vals (The Last Waltz, Dir. Martin Scorsese, 1978) (23/10/2026) Documental del concierto de despedida de The Band en el Winterland de San Francisco en 1976, con actuaciones de Bob Dylan, Neil Young, Van Morrison, Eric Clapton, Joni Mitchell, Muddy Waters y muchos más. Scorsese filmó con varios equipos de cine lo que se considera el mejor documental de rock de la historia.

Silencio (Silence, Dir. Martin Scorsese, 2016) (23/10/2026) Dos sacerdotes jesuitas portugueses del siglo XVII viajan a Japón para buscar a su mentor desaparecido, y se enfrentan a la brutal persecución de los cristianos por parte del gobierno Tokugawa. Una meditación profunda y austera sobre la fe, el martirio y el silencio de Dios. Con Andrew Garfield, Adam Driver y Liam Neeson.

The Chronology of Water (The Chronology of Water, Dir. Kristen Stewart, 2025) (30/10/2026) ESTRENO ESTA SEMANA EN MUBI Debut en la dirección de la actriz Kristen Stewart, presentado en la sección Un Certain Regard del Festival de Cannes 2025. Adaptación de las memorias autobiográficas de Lidia Yuknavitch: una joven que crece en un entorno marcado por la violencia y el alcohol y encuentra en la natación y la escritura dos vías de escape. La película rechaza la narración cronológica y sumerge al espectador en una corriente de imágenes, frases, recuerdos y sensaciones. Producida por Ridley Scott y la propia Stewart. Con Imogen Poots, Thora Birch, Tom Sturridge y Jim Belushi.

Esta cercanía (This Closeness, Dir. Kit Zauhar, 2024) (30/10/2026) ESTRENO ESTA SEMANA EN MUBI En Filadelfia, Tessa y Ben, una pareja en crisis, alquilan una habitación en el apartamento de Adam, un joven solitario y recluido que se convierte en testigo involuntario de los momentos más privados de su relación. El encierro en ese espacio diminuto desencadena una batalla íntima por el territorio, el afecto y los límites. Estrenada en SXSW 2023, con 91% en Rotten Tomatoes.

Tendaberry (Tendaberry, Dir. Haley Elizabeth Anderson, 2024) (30/10/2026) ESTRENO ESTA SEMANA EN MUBI Dakota tiene 23 años y vive en el Brooklyn de inmigrantes de Coney Island y Brighton Beach. Cuando su novio regresa a Ucrania para cuidar a su padre enfermo, ella debe enfrentarse a la precariedad de aferrarse al pasado mientras forja su futuro en solitario. Estrenada en la sección Next del Festival de Sundance 2024.

Estrenos de series en Mubi (octubre 2026)

La noche que Logan despertó (La nuit où Laurier Gaudreault s’est réveillé / The Night Logan Woke Up) (15/10/2026) Primera serie creada, escrita y dirigida por Xavier Dolan (Mamá, Matthias & Maxime), en la que también actúa. En octubre de 1991, un suceso terrible sacude a una familia de Lac Saint-Jean, Quebec: Logan viola a Mimi, de 14 años, en una noche que rompe para siempre la amistad entre dos familias. Treinta años después, Mimi —ahora tanatóloga de renombre— regresa al pueblo para velar el cuerpo de su madre y se reencuentra con todos. Los rencores y los secretos enterrados resurgen con una fuerza devastadora. Cinco episodios. Adaptación de la obra teatral de Michel Marc Bouchard, con Anne Dorval, Julie LeBreton y Patrick Hivon. Banda sonora de Hans Zimmer y David Fleming. Presentada en Sundance 2023.

"Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展陈路线按时间顺序划分为十个单元，其布景气势恢弘，旨在重现作品原本保存或为其专门构思的各种环境。正如第一个展厅具有毋庸置疑的视觉冲击力，展出了圣母领报小回廊的大幅壁画，这些壁画被嵌入到修士圣母领报大殿的回廊拱门之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正是从这个第一展厅开始，人们可以立即感受到16世纪初佛罗伦萨共和国的艺术交流与文化氛围，安德烈亚·德尔·萨托（《圣母的诞生》）、罗索·菲奥伦蒂诺（《圣母升天》）和我们的主角（《圣母往见》，1514-1516年）得以在此密切合作。在这种气候中，我们已经可以追踪到蓬托尔莫的艺术渊源，他密切关注拉斐尔，尤其是米开朗琪罗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Pontormo_14767.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "蓬托尔莫，展览现场，奎里纳莱马厩艺术宫，2026 – 2027年，摄影：阿尔贝托·诺韦利", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，切莫忘记，就在1515年，年仅21岁的蓬托尔莫曾因学习原因前往罗马，与米开朗琪罗的宏伟气势（西斯廷礼拜堂于1512年落成）以及拉斐尔的优雅（拉斐尔的前两间画室已于当年完工）迎面相遇。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Bronzino-Ritratto-di-dama-in-rosso.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "布龙齐诺 红衣贵妇肖像 1532年前后 布面油画，89,8 × 70,5 cm © 法兰克福施泰德博物馆", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "从加卢佐修道院到卡蓬尼小堂：蓬托尔莫的杰作", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "引人入胜的是加卢佐修道院（Certosa del Galluzzo）大回廊中《基督受难史》（Storie della Passione di Cristo）壁画的展示。1522年起，他为躲避波及佛罗伦萨的强烈瘟疫，曾与年轻助手布龙齐诺（Bronzino）一同避难于此：他在这里创作了五幅拱顶壁画，其中有四幅在本次展览中展出。尽管长期暴露于恶劣天气在一定程度上损害了其原初的色彩，但人们依然能从中读出整个布局的宏伟气势。这一布局深受阿尔布雷希特·丢勒（Albrecht Dürer）版画的影响，这让他遭到了瓦萨里的严厉批评，因为他抛弃了“良好的意大利风格”，而采用了“德国风格”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Pontormo_sala4.jpg", "alt": "蓬托尔莫展览马厩", "caption": "蓬托尔莫，展览现场，奎里纳尔马厩美术馆，2026 – 2027，摄影：阿尔贝托·诺韦利（Alberto Novelli）", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同样迷人的是专门展示为卡波尼小堂（Cappella Capponi）创作的作品的展厅，其中包括著名的所谓《卡波尼哀悼基督》（Pietà Capponi）。尽管该作品呈现出浓厚的米开朗基罗和拉斐尔风格影响，但它凝聚了蓬托尔莫的全部独创性——除了将其假想导师的影响推向极致（包括采用完全不自然的色彩系列，如变幻的粉红色、星际蓝、酸绿色和磷光橙，且没有真实的阴影），他还彻底摆脱了与该主题相关的绘画常规，构建了一种完全前所未有的建筑结构，这甚至给这幅祭坛画的命名本身带来了困难，因为它缺乏将其归入特定类别所需的那些细节。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Pontormo_14752.jpg", "alt": "蓬托尔莫展览马厩", "caption": "蓬托尔莫，展览现场，奎里纳尔马厩美术馆，2026 – 2027，摄影：阿尔贝托·诺韦利（Alberto Novelli）", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这里既没有十字架，也没有墓穴，因此它不可能是《耶稣下十字架》（Deposizione）；基督也不在圣母的膝头，所以它不可能是《哀悼基督》（Pietà）。然而，抛开这些争论不谈，这幅祭坛画的宏伟气势依然存在，它带有旋转且悬浮的动感，暗示着一种音乐般的律动：也许正因如此，那些没有翅膀的“天使”才会微微张开嘴唇注视着我们，仿佛在伴随着乐长（Maestro di Cappella）的指挥手势吟唱着赞美诗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Pontormo-Visitazione-SS.Annunziata.jpg", "alt": "蓬托尔莫展览马厩", "caption": "蓬托尔莫（Jacopo da Pontormo）《圣母访亲》，1514-1516年 剥离壁画，408 × 338 cm 佛罗伦萨，圣母领报大殿 宗教建筑基金会财产，宗教事务与宗教建筑基金会管理中央局，内政部", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "《圣母访亲》与蓬托尔莫在佛罗伦萨文艺复兴中的遗产：一场犹如旅行般的展览", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种独创性在作为展览路线尾声的同样前所未见的《圣母访亲》（Visitazione）版本中也得到了体现。它将全部注意力集中在圣母与伊丽莎白（Elisabetta）的拥抱上，不再以唤起玛丽表姐住所的古典建筑为背景，而是将其置于一条佛罗伦萨的街道上。两名几乎等身大小的女性形象并肩而立，然而她们却望向观众，带着那种几乎惊愕的表情，类似于先前作品中的表情，这看起来更像是一种署名、一种戏剧面具或是一个歌唱的瞬间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，通过观察准备稿可以发现这种转变，它不仅完美地展现了一些微小的变化是如何赋予这四人组合更强大的力量和表现力的，还展示了面部是如何变得更加宏伟、充满活力和表现力的（让人怎能不想起雅各布·托里蒂 [Jacopo Torriti] 呢？）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Pontormo_sala5b.jpg", "alt": "蓬托尔莫展览马厩", "caption": "蓬托尔莫，展览现场，奎里纳尔马厩美术馆，2026 – 2027，摄影：阿尔贝托·诺韦利（Alberto Novelli）", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，这场展览不仅是对这位佛罗伦萨天才的深入探究之旅，也标志着一次穿梭于他所处时代的旅程——与他的导师、同伴和弟子们同行，凸显了美第奇家族圈子内部产生的关键艺术联盟。为了丰富和完善展览路线，除了收藏在不同地点的84件蓬托尔莫的绘画、壁画和素描作品外，还展出了大约50件艺术史上的其他巨匠的作品，例如画家的密友罗索·菲奥伦蒂诺（Rosso Fiorentino）、其恩师安德烈·德尔·萨尔托（Andrea del Sarto），以及皮耶罗·迪·科西莫（Piero di Cosimo）、布龙齐诺和米开朗基罗。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Correva l’anno 1956 quando fu presentata Pontormo e il primo manierismo fiorentino , la prima importante monografica, allestita a Palazzo Strozzi e curata dallo studioso Luciano Berti , sul fondamentale e geniale Pontormo , al secolo Jacopo Carucci da Pontorme (Pontormo, Empoli, 1494 – Firenze, 1557). A 70 anni da quella occasione, fuori dal territorio di Firenze, le Scuderie del Quirinale propongono al grande pubblico, visitabile fino al 7 febbraio 2027 , una muscolosa mostra sul rivoluzionario “fiorentino” che, nel pieno del Rinascimento, spezzò tutti i canoni artistici della sua epoca, divenendo una delle figure chiave della “maniera” e, quindi, della straordinaria stagione del Manierismo.

Pontormo oltre Vasari: la riscoperta di un maestro del Manierismo

Una figura cardine che ancora oggi, nonostante i numerosi studi compiuti sulla sua ineguagliabile produzione, risente del riduttivo giudizio di Giorgio Vasari , che ne scrive in entrambe le versioni de Le vite de’ più eccellenti pittori, scultori e architettori . Tuttavia, è solo in quella del 1568 – che vede il Nostro scomparso da poco meno di una decina di anni – che gli dedica una biografia autonoma (in quella del 1550 era all’interno della biografia di Andrea del Sarto ), ponendolo subito dopo Cristofano Gherardi detto Doceno e prima di Simone Mosca . È qui che il Vasari aggiunge quei dettagli caratteriali che influiranno sull’apprezzamento del valore del corpus artistico del Pontormo nei secoli successivi.

Tanto che, nel Settecento, nessuno si fece scrupolo di distruggere il ciclo di affreschi del coro della Basilica di San Lorenzo a Firenze, cui l’artista si era dedicato per ben dieci anni, durante i radicali lavori di ristrutturazione promossi da Anna Maria Luisa de’ Medici e compiuti dall’architetto Ferdinando Ruggieri. Stessa indifferenza mostrata anche per la decorazione della volta della Cappella Capponi nella Chiesa di Santa Felicita. L’Aretino lo descrive come un uomo stravagante, cupo e solitario, accusandolo di aver abbandonato la “buona via” michelangiolesca per inseguire lo stile nordico di Dürer , «…e fu tanto pauroso della morte, che non voleva, non che altro, udirne ragionare, e fuggiva l’avere a incontrare i morti», influenzando negativamente la percezione della sua salute mentale e della sua arte per secoli.

Bisogna, infatti, attendere gli studi del Novecento di Frederick Mortimer Clapp prima e Roberto Longhi poi, per vederne riconosciuti l’indiscusso talento e la profonda portata artistica, tanto da influenzare artisti a noi più vicini come Pier Paolo Pasolini e Bill Viola . Eppure, alcuni pregiudizi, tuttora, condizionano la lettura di certi suoi lavori, interpretati ancora in base a quei dettagli biografici fissati dal Vasari.

La mostra di Pontormo a Roma: 84 opere alle Scuderie del Quirinale

Curata da Cristina Acidini — tra le maggiori conoscitrici del Rinascimento e del Manierismo mediceo — insieme a una squadra di altissimo livello, composta da Elena Capretti, Philippe Costamagna, Bruce Edelstein e Carlo Falciani , la monografica ha tratto notevole vantaggio nell’essere ospitata nelle Scuderie del Quirinale, per la sicura agevolazione dei prestiti di opere fondamentali che, altrimenti, non avrebbero avuto la garanzia di una copertura di sicurezza totale.

Un percorso espositivo suddiviso in dieci sezioni sviluppate cronologicamente, con un allestimento portentoso, teso a ricreare le diverse ambientazioni in cui le opere sono conservate o per le quali erano state concepite. Come la prima sala, di indiscusso impatto, che ospita gli estesi affreschi del Chiostrino dei Voti, inseriti in quelli che erano gli archi del Chiostro nel venerato santuario della Santissima Annunziata dei frati serviti.

E proprio da questa prima sala, immediatamente si percepiscono sia gli scambi artistici nonché l’atmosfera culturale della Firenze Repubblicana nei primi anni del Cinquecento, dove poterono lavorare a stretto contatto Andrea del Sarto ( La Natività della Vergine ), Rosso Fiorentino ( Assunzione di Maria ) e il Nostro ( Visitazione , 1514-1516). In tale temperie già si rintracciano i riferimenti artistici di Pontormo, che guarda da vicino Raffaello e, in particolar modo, Michelangelo .

Non bisogna infatti dimenticare che il Nostro, proprio nel 1515, ad appena 21 anni, si era recato a Roma per motivi di studio, trovandosi a faccia a faccia con la monumentalità michelangiolesca – la Cappella Sistina era stata inaugurata nel 1512 – e la grazia raffaellesca – in quell’anno erano già state completate le prime due Stanze di Raffaello.

Dalla Certosa del Galluzzo alla Cappella Capponi: i capolavori di Pontormo

Suggestiva è la presentazione degli affreschi delle Storie della Passione di Cristo nel Chiostro Grande nella Certosa del Galluzzo dove, dal 1522, si era rifugiato, insieme al giovane aiutante Bronzino , per fuggire dalla virulenta epidemia di peste che aveva toccato anche Firenze: ha qui realizzato cinque lunette e ben quattro sono presenti in mostra. Nonostante la lunga esposizione alle intemperie ne abbia in qualche modo compromesso l’originale cromia, tuttavia è ancora possibile leggere la maestosità dell’intero impianto. Un impianto fortemente influenzato dalle incisioni di Albrecht Dürer, che gli costò la dura critica del Vasari, perché aveva abbandonato “La buona maniera italiana” e adottato lo “Stile tedesco”.

Altrettanto seducente è la sala dedicata alle opere realizzate per la Cappella Capponi, tra cui la celeberrima cosiddetta Pietà Capponi la quale, sebbene presenti forti influenze michelangiolesche e raffaellesche, condensa tutta l’originalità di Pontormo che, oltre a portare alle estreme conseguenze proprio gli influssi dei suoi maestri putativi (tra cui i colori con una gamma cromatica del tutto innaturale, rosa cangianti, azzurri siderali, verdi acido e arancioni fosforici, privi di ombreggiature reali), si libera completamente dagli schemi pittorici legati al tema e costruisce un’architettura completamente inedita, così da creare difficoltà nella denominazione stessa della Pala, perché mancante di quei dettagli necessari per inquadrarla in una determinata categoria.

Non ci sono né la Croce né il Sepolcro, quindi non può essere una Deposizione ; Cristo non è sul grembo della Vergine, perciò non può essere una Pietà . Ma, tralasciando queste discettazioni, resta la grandiosità di questa pala, con il suo moto rotatorio e sospeso, che suggerisce un movimento musicale: forse per questo gli “angeli” – senza ali – guardano verso di noi, con le labbra socchiuse, per seguire le indicazioni del Maestro di Cappella mentre intonano un inno.

La Visitazione e l’eredità di Pontormo nel Rinascimento fiorentino: una mostra viaggio

Quell’originalità che si coglie anche nell’altrettanto inedita versione della Visitazione , che chiude il percorso espositivo. Ponendo la totale attenzione all’abbraccio tra la Vergine ed Elisabetta, non più davanti a un’architettura classica evocante l’abitazione della cugina di Maria, bensì in una strada fiorentina. A grandezza pressoché naturale, sono affiancate due figure femminili che, però, guardano verso lo spettatore, con quell’espressione quasi attonita, simile a quella delle precedenti opere, che appare più come una sigla o una sorta di maschera teatrale oppure il momento di un canto.

Lo scarto, infatti, si può rintracciare osservando il disegno preparatorio che indica perfettamente non solo come alcune piccole variazioni abbiano dato maggiore potenza e intensità al quartetto, ma anche come i volti fossero più monumentali, energici e espressivi (come non pensare a Jacopo Torriti ?).

Una mostra, dunque, che non solo rappresenta un profondo percorso sul genio fiorentino ma, altresì, scandisce un viaggio attraverso l’epoca in cui egli visse, insieme ai suoi maestri, compagni e discepoli, mettendo in evidenza i cruciali sodalizi artistici nati all’interno della cerchia medicea. A integrare e completare il percorso espositivo, infatti, insieme a 84 tra dipinti, affreschi e disegni di Pontormo custoditi in siti differenti, anche una cinquantina di opere di altri grandi della storia dell’arte, come Rosso Fiorentino, stretto amico del Nostro, Andrea del Sarto, suo maestro, e di Piero di Cosimo, Bronzino e Michelangelo.

article_text:
I didn’t know before reading your new memoir that you were almost Tony Soprano. Is there a role that you really wanted that you didn’t end up getting?

It’s not Tony Soprano. There is not a role that I didn’t get that I ever gave more than four hours of grievance to. When I don’t get something, I move on. Because there’s no point. I’m very pragmatic that way. It’s for your own mental health. Once it’s gone, it’s gone.

The thing you have to understand is if you don’t get something, it’s not personal. It can be as simple as the director has already got three brunettes or three male actors and they don’t need a fourth. It’s never personally about you. It’s about the picture they have in their head … Or sometimes a role is already out to another actor and they’re just waiting for them to say yes. That is one thing I wish they wouldn’t do, because that’s a waste of my time. If you’ve got an offer out to Ben Affleck or whoever, don’t put me on the revolving wheel of possibility. Because if I find out, I’m not doing it. Not that they care! [laughs]

If you were casting your dream project with three actors you’ve already worked with, plus one new face, who would be on your team?

Allison Janney. Kerry Armstrong. Alison Whyte. And a new face … I just saw Moneyball and I don’t think I ever took Brad Pitt that seriously but that guy is phenomenal. Great movie .

Acting opposite Janney in A View from the Bridge on Broadway sounds as though it was a transcendental experience for you.

It was. That’s the thing about Arthur Miller’s plays: the women are the glue. The women make the plays work. My performance is not going to be enough to make it work – I’ve been so lucky to have two phenomenal women [Janney and Whyte in Death of a Salesman] play the lead roles with me. Without them, you have no play.

Your account of your years working on Without a Trace is really fascinating – that era of network television where they were making 24, 25, 26 episodes a season feels like a bygone time. Would you ever do a show like that again?

If I did, I would approach it completely differently. I would not get involved in quality control. I would figure out the lines that didn’t work for me, change them and get on with it …

When I wrote an episode it totally transformed relationship with the writers because I suddenly realised how difficult it was to write a story that gets chopped into four pieces, where you have to pause for five minutes of commercials then come back and re-engage your audience. Very difficult. When I wrote the first one [LaPaglia wrote two episodes], I went, “Oh god, I need to go and apologise to some of these guys!”

The workload on Without a Trace was counterproductive to doing good work. I would find myself acting on autopilot. I’d have the new episode that we were shooting next week sitting in my chair. The minute I finished doing a take, I’d go, “Right, bring in the writers, I’m going to talk to them for a minute.” Then we’d go back and do another take. Then they’d come in and I’d start talking about the next episode and what I think they should fix. It was like being schizophrenic … And at the end of it, I realised the show would have been successful whether I did that or not. So annoying. I wish I’d known that when I started.

Which role has been most personally fulfilling for you, and why?

Lantana . From the minute that I read it, I was in love with it. There wasn’t a single word in that script that I wanted to change, which is so unusual for me. Andrew Bovell wrote an absolutely lean, suspenseful script and we basically shot it exactly as he wrote it – that’s very rare. The preparation I got to do [to play a Sydney police detective] was incredible. It was some of the funniest stuff and some of the most heartbreaking stuff, in a way. I ended up being placed with these two Sydney detectives who were themselves under investigation. They were eventually found guilty, of course. They were the funniest guys, though. I remember they took me to Leichhardt once and everybody knew them. They didn’t pay for a single meal, ever, when I was there.

As someone who is also from Adelaide, I laughed out loud at your descriptions of the city, like: “There’s a bad energy running through it. Whenever I go back, I feel the same low-frequency unease that used to spook me as a kid.” Have your feelings about it changed at all?

A little bit. Not drastically. Remember, I’m talking about an Adelaide that I left a very long time ago. I was there recently working [on Death of a Salesman] and the Adelaide audiences were amazing. I didn’t feel Adelaide had changed all that much itself but I was greatly appreciative of the audiences. They were some of the most raucous. They laughed much more than other audiences did. Because there’s a dark streak in Adelaide, which I appreciated.

If a biopic was made about your life, who would play you?

God, that’s such an awkward question. Channing Tatum!

You write about ageing into playing Willy Loman. Are there any theatre roles that loom large for you as you grow older?

Anyone who’s written for a 67-year-old. There’s not many! I’m not a big wishlist guy. I’m much more in the moment. I’m a gun for hire. I’ve tried to self-generate projects and I found that to be an incredibly difficult and boring experience. I have no capacity to raise money. I can’t ask somebody to put money into a project that I know they’re going to lose money on. And they will! I’ve been the person that’s lost money. I’ve done the cardinal sin of investing in my own projects and I’ve lost so much money! And it doesn’t matter what contract you sign, either. You can sign a contract that says first dollar repayment, then they lie and cook the books. It’s happened to me more than once. Mostly with Australian films.

It is so much harder to get anything financed in Australia, right?

Well, they’re better at cooking the books. [laughs]

What is the best piece of advice you have ever received?

“Know your lines and don’t hit the furniture.” That is Spencer Tracy’s acting advice. I’ve always thought, dead on.

What has been your most memorable interaction with a fan?

This one was at a distance, which I liked. It was quite early in my career. I was walking down Sixth Avenue in New York, which is quite a wide avenue, and I hear from the other side: “Hey, LaPaglia!” I went, “Yeah?” And the guy says, “I hate you! I hate every movie that you’re in!” And I went, “Good for you. You have taste!” He laughed, I laughed and on we went.

That’s what I liked about New York back then. People just had no filter. My daughter lives there now and I always thought I’d end up back there. But having gone back to see my daughter a few times in New York, there’s only three good months a year in New York. Summer’s too hot. Winter’s miserable. I like California now.

But also I’m pretty sure I’m going to move to Mexico shortly. It is more to ride out Trump than anything. There’s no way that he’s going to let an election happen. I think you’re going to see some significant outbreaks of civil unrest. And do you know what? I’d just rather not be there for that.

I don’t like Trump but he’s quite old and he won’t be around much longer. That’s the saving grace. Once he goes, that whole party falls to pieces. The only thing that keeps it together is the cult of Trump. There’s all these people behind Trump that actually run the country and they won’t have that cover any more. They’re not very brave, they don’t want to put themselves out in the open – but Trump keeps outing them! [laughs] That’s one thing I like about him: he has no filter. He has no loyalty to anyone but himself. The idea that he thinks his son is going to run and win is a joke. His son is one of the most dislikable humans on Earth. Even more dislikable than Donald. At least Donald’s funny!

Do you have a nemesis? (And based on your memoir: is it John Landis ?)

As you get older, those things count less. I don’t have the energy for that any more. I don’t think I would have considered John Landis a nemesis. I just did not understand him. I still don’t understand him! I’m not the only person that’s clashed with him but there are other people who swear by him. I just can’t respond to screaming. He screams a lot and that bothers me. It’s unnecessary and off-putting on a set. He may not do that any more, it was a long time ago. But I have read things where he said, “I don’t understand why he doesn’t like me” and I found it remarkable that he doesn’t understand. Maybe he doesn’t register that stuff. I’ll certainly won’t forget it! I’m just waiting for the lawsuit.

The Life We Choose by Anthony LaPaglia is published on 27 October (HarperCollins)

article_text:
Those holding the purse strings in Spanish film and TV must not “reject” ambitious projects or they could miss the next La Bola Negra or Sîrat , according to the influential former content chief at Movistar Plus+ .

Domingo Corral whipped a partisan audience into something of a frenzy at the MIA Market in Rome yesterday when he passionately called on TV and film commissioners to do away with safety-first tendencies and embrace the spirit that he attempted to install at Movistar Plus+, the pay TV and streaming arm of Telefonica-owned Spanish telco Movistar.

Corral was joined on the MIA panel by Maria Zamora from Elastica Films , Belén Atienza from Suspense Entertainment and Fernando Bovaira from Mod Producciones , who all agreed that recent upticks at the Spanish box office could be attributed to ambitious but mainstream movies.

Related Stories

Marco Bassetti Says Banijay Has Spent $1.1B On "Creativity" In Four Years But Warns U.S. Giants Must Reward European Producers

Edward Berger Says Movie Biz "Needed Netflix To Wake Up" But Studios Can Now "Inspire" The Streamer

“Formulaic, conservative proposals will always be there, but you cannot reject the other way,” said Corral. Bovaira, who has produced films such as Agora and Vanilla Sky , added: “We need commissioners who are willing to go the casino and gamble.”

Watch on Deadline

Recalling his strategy during his 11-year spell at Movistar, Corral added: “If there was ambition with the producer, we had to make sure the vision became a reality. We wanted vision and passion for something original, and the role of the commissioner was key. As an independent producer now, if you don’t have a strong commissioner who promotes the strategy, it’s very difficult.”

Corral and his team were axed from Movistar Plus+ last year, prompting an outcry from the creative community, who saw his outlook as the main preserve of ambitious but popular storytelling. His track record included La Bola Negra , which has just released in four screens in the U.S. to $278,000 ahead of its streaming launch.

Corral also greenlit Cannes title Sîrat from Oliver Laxe, Los Tigres from Alberto Rodríguez, Alauda Ruiz de Azúa’s Los Domingos , and Cinco Minutos Más , starring and written by Berto Romero and helmed by Javier Ruiz Calder.

Soon after news of his axing got out, Around 150 creatives, heavyweights Pedro Almodóvar, Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruzan, signed an open letter thanking Corral and his team for championing high-end original film and TV and asking for those efforts to continue and standards be maintained.

Movistar Plus+’s Head of Original Films & Spanish Cinema, Guillermo Farré, later told Deadline he was committed to staying the course on original Spanish films, but not everyone is convinced yet.

During the MIA panel, Zamora from Elastica, which is selling La Bola Negra , said: “When you want to make authors grow with you, it’s difficult to raise the funding you need for them to really perform internationally. We don’t know if Movistar will keep doing it. We hope they will.”

Corral was keen to push the concept of ‘quality mainstream,’ which is predicated on the idea that ambitious concepts will attract audiences on the strength of the content.

“When I was at Movistar Plus our obsession was how to be and how to stay relevant in a context where there are so many films and series that get made,” he said. “If you follow the algorithm it’s a surefire way of not being relevant, in my opinion.

“The strategy we followed may not work for everyone but it worked for us. We had three films in Cannes in three years, and we had the support of the entire industry and without the producers we could not have done it.”

Corral has since struck a production deal with HBO Max , and this week told Deadline why he believes his vision of ambition production aligns with that of Sarah Aubrey and Casey Bloys at the top of the merger Skydance commissioning tree. The debut show from the pact, about the disappearance of Spanish petty criminal El Nani, remains in development, Corral confirmed.

The MIA Market in Rome runs through Friday.

デザイナー・圷イサクによる新プロジェクト『shuku+ga（祝＋我）』の第一弾として、展示・受注販売会が代官山 ALにて開催される。

本プロジェクトのテーマは、「なんにもない日に、おめでとう。」自分と大切な誰かを祝うことを起点に、写真家・川島小鳥が、田辺あゆみ、TAEHEONら10名の飾らない姿と、その場に流れる時間を撮り下ろした。会場では、川島小鳥によるポートレートとともに、圷が手がけた3種のネックレス、松井正憲（METER）がデザインしたZINEとアートポスターを展示する。会期中は、これらを組み合わせたセットの受注販売も実施する予定だ。読む、部屋に飾る、身につける。それぞれの作品が、ひとつの空間のなかでつながる展示となっている。

初日の9月25日（金）17:00からはレセプションを開催予定。ぜひ足をお運びいただきたい。

タイトル

『shuku+ga（祝＋我）』なんにもない日に、おめでとう。

場所

AL（東京都渋谷区恵比寿南 3-7-17）

会期

2026年9月25日（金）〜27日（日）

時間

9月25日：15:00〜20:00 ＊17:00 よりレセプションを予定（どなたでも参加いただけます） 9月26日、27日：11:00〜19:00

入場料

無料

article_text:
The Tokyo International Film Festival ’s Tokyo Talk program presented a masterclass with Zeze Takahisa , director of the festival’s opening film, “Sukiyaki.”

Held before a full-house crowd at Tokyo Midtown Hibiya, the talk focused on Zeze’s early “pink” (softcore porn) and indie films, followed by questions about his more recent work.

Born in 1960 in Oita Prefecture, Zeze joined a pink film production company in 1986 and worked as an assistant director. He made his directorial debut in 1989 with “Extracurricular Activity: Rape,” for which he won the Pink Grand Prix Award for Best New Director. Together with Sano Kazuhiro, Sato Toshiki and Sato Hisayasu, Zeze was hailed as one of the “Four Heavenly Kings of Pink.”

Related Stories

Pink films screened in specialized theaters for an exclusively male audience, and directors had to insert a bed scene every 10 minutes or so. “I’ve always been pretty firm in my convictions,” said Zeze. “Starting from the early 1990s the culture shifted and I had more freedom to say what I wanted. That kind of thing was important to me.”

At the time, Zeze was interested in stories about female criminals. “It’s just different from the male perspective,” he said. “The motives behind the crimes and so on. I found it fascinating.”

Scripted by Zeze, “Extracurricular Activity: Rape” was about delinquent high school girls who hang out at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport and battle the yakuza. Zeze gave it the “private” title “Go to Haneda and You Will See Kids Dressed Like Pirates Ready to Attack.”

Asked about a 1994 pink, “Genuine Lesbians: Embarrassing Positions” (Zeze’s own title: “Fallen Angels in September”), Zeze said the film, which was about female soulmates, reflected the interest he described as “this whole mysticism thing” shared by many young people then. “Searching for past lives became a sort of trend, and people started seeking connections to this different world,” he added. “I thought that maybe I could make a movie centered around something like that.”

Zeze said the “Four Heavenly Kings” moniker came from a pink theater “in Toyama – or maybe Ishikawa – I can’t remember.” It reminded Zeze and the other “kings” of “Nouvelle Vague” – a tag that gave critical and commercial cachet to its members. “So we figured that, rather than work as individuals, we should debut under a group name,” he said. “We decided to use the ‘Four Heavenly Kings’ label to our advantage.”

The “kings” films were also shown in retrospectives at the Rotterdam festival and elsewhere abroad. “Actually, the overseas reception came first, and then it was sort of re-imported” back to Japan, Zeze said.

Meanwhile, in Japan, the “kings” and other pink film directors still had to incorporate a certain amount of eros. “No one was telling us to stop doing these politically sensitive things,” said Zeze. “It was just wonderful… there really was a lot of freedom back then.”

Also, pink film directors were not confined to a porn ghetto. “Things weren’t standardized back then,” Zeze said. “I worked with directors from my generation who had diverse backgrounds, like Aoyama Shinji and Suzuki Takuji. We’d get together either because we’d met by chance or because we wanted to create something interesting.”

In 1997 Zeze made his mainstream debut with the teen horror “Kokkuri-san” but continued to alternate between pink and mainstream films for the next decade.

In 2010 he released his most ambitious film to date, “Heaven’s Story,” a 278-minute revenge drama that screened in the Forum section of the Berlin Film Festival, where it won the FIPRESCI Prize.

“It was different from a so-called ‘ordinary movie,’” Zeze said. “I’d been working on commercial films until then, but I realized I had to do something else. Personally, I felt a sense of urgency – or maybe a sense of crisis – that things weren’t going well, and that’s what pushed me to take on this challenge.”

There’s a lot of talk, Zeze said, about how difficult it is to make a film unless it’s adapted from source material. “But the movies we actually found interesting or the ones I personally found entertaining were all originals.”

Zeze himself has made commercial films with stories sourced from existing IP, such as the hit 2016 two-part mystery/suspense “64,” which was based on a bestselling novel, but said, “The industry is too focused on the ‘source material market.’ They think that if the source material is selling well, they should adapt it.”

“So I feel that pursuing original concepts and making original films is incredibly important right now,” he added. “They have a unique, compelling strength.”

article_text:
Hatted heads crowd the frame. Tweed overcoats. A cigarette burning down in the front row. Hastings Park, 16 July 1955 carries the bite of a press photograph, and the bite is what gives it away: too crisp, too saturated for the year it claims. Stan Douglas, a Vancouver native, speaks of the scene he staged down to the last extra: “The guy on the bottom left is telling off-colour jokes and the woman is clearly offended.” Beneath the smut lies the social anatomy. This racetrack crowd embodies postwar consumerism, “people who were making things being able to buy those things, a sort of perpetual motion machine for capitalism.”

Vancouver has been his laboratory for forty years, its institutional failures his raw material. Abbott & Cordova, 7 August 1971 restages the Gastown riot as nocturnal choreography of an almost indecent beauty: streetlamps, red bodywork, bodies strewn across wet asphalt. Hippies were squatting the warehouses then, to the displeasure of a police force that, as the artist tells it, “would rather keep the communities quarantined.” The print mounts the riot squad’s charge and declines to take sides: “It’s basically there, installed in that location, so you can observe, wonder what happened to this place, and start a conversation.”

Breakdown holds him more than catastrophe. “Typically in almost all of my work, I’m looking at conditions where something has broken down,” he says. “These events, these ruptures, these breakings of habits, are times in which possibilities are found.” Now and then he takes the idea at its word. “Scenes from the Blackout” imagines what a photographer might have caught while the power failures held New York still. In Solitaire , a woman sits on the bare boards of an elevator shaft, an oil lamp her only light.

Thwarted promises come next. “Disco Angola” binds the broke New York of the early 1970s, where dancing passed for escape, to a freshly decolonized Angola. In Two Friends, 1975 , a woman in coral and a man in mint green pose among a club’s gilt moldings, beautiful and already in mourning. The picture carries the gloss of a fashion editorial, and the gloss is the point. Lodged inside it are two confiscated freedoms: disco swallowed by the market, Angolan independence ground down by the Cold War. “Utopias may not last long,” he allows. “But what remains is a model of how a positive future could have taken place.”

Then the means swell. “2011 ≠ 1848” rebuilds the uprisings of Tunis, Hackney, and the Brooklyn Bridge out of press archives and social media. “Penn Station’s Half Century” raises the station razed in 1963 in a light only computer-generated imagery can furnish. A single obsession drives the whole enterprise: “Almost all of the works address moments when history could have gone one way or another. We live in the residue of such moments.” In an age of generative images, such virtuosity unsettles. What it lays bare is how long photography has been arranging the world, and how openly Stan Douglas does his arranging.

An entire gallery belongs to Birth of a Nation , shown in France for the first time. The installation takes apart the chase sequence from D.W. Griffith’s film, the racist epic that single-handedly revived the Ku Klux Klan. Douglas follows the bloodline and finds the descendants where nobody thinks to look: “Mickey, for example, has a black body, wears white gloves and like Jim Crow is prone to convulsive movements that mix the cruelty of his stereotype with laughter.”

Five screens share one wall. Griffith holds the center, ringed by four new vantage points, among them two invented characters whom young Flora collapses into a single terror. The sequence mesmerizes exactly as the original did, then withdraws the pleasure. The hanging turns to color, the rope drops against a blue screen, the actor’s feet find the floor of a present-day studio. The frame widens. A crew member walks a horse toward the wide door, opens it, and goes out into the light. The air comes in.

“Parallax” runs at the Jeu de Paume through January 10, 2027.

Rest》是对这些挥之不去思绪的发掘，是对释放、臣服以及背负着无法撤销之重生活的意义的探索。这一系列作品诞生于不眠之夜以及渴望与接纳之间的原始空间。通过这件作品，我审视了那些将我与尚未治愈的振动捆绑在一起的物体、情感和叙事。每个物体都变成了一种释放的仪式，对无常的献祭，以及一门学会与悲伤共存而非战胜悲伤的静谧课程。它的核心是悲伤：它如何挥之不去，如何转变，以及我们如何学会带着它前行。我被坚守与放手之间的张力、悲伤与爱的交织方式，以及治愈并非终点而是一个持续解构过程的理念所吸引。在这个空间里，我邀请观众反思他们自己的依恋，思考他们仍在承载着什么，以及他们可能终于准备好将什么安放于平静之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的作品探索无形之物，包括记忆、梦境，以及现实与想象之间变幻的空间。我被那些挥之不去的碎片所吸引，例如代际传承的故事、稍纵即逝的时刻，以及被记住的事物与被遗忘的事物之间模糊的界限。通过摄影、纺织品和雕塑，我创造出了让看不见和未说出口之物成形的场域。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在秘鲁和德国移民父母的抚养下，我在美墨边境长大地，这种背景赋予了我贯穿整个创作实践的一种“中间态”意识。最初对文化身份的探究，已经演变为对边缘性（liminality）更广泛的探索，审视着归属与疏离、在场与缺席、以及个人与集体之间的门槛。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", What began as an exploration of cultural identity has expanded into a broader investigation of liminality, absence, and the ways memory and longing shape how we connect to ourselves and others."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lesley earned her BFA in Fine Art Photography from Texas State University in 2021, and her work has been shown nationally at institutions such as Houston Center for Photography, Touchstone Gallery, and Humble Arts Foundation. She has participated in residencies such as LATITUDE (Chicago, IL), Vermont Studio Center (Johnson, VT), Château d’Orquevaux (France), KUNSTRAUM (Brooklyn, NY), and Kala Art Institute (Berkeley, CA)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "She is currently a member of ICOSA, an artist-run collective gallery in Austin, TX."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Follow Chantal on Instagram: @chantallesley", "links": [{"text": "@chantallesley", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/chantallesley/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Chantal-Lesley-Let-the-Quiet-Hold-It.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Chantal Lesley, Let the Quiet Hold It"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As I Lay It All To Rest"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We carry so much within us: Memories, regrets, unspoken words, and lingering ghosts that echo in the quiet hours of the night. As I Lay It All to Rest is an excavation of these restless thoughts, an exploration of what it means to release, to surrender, and to live with the weight of what cannot be undone. This body of work emerges from sleepless nights and the raw space between longing and acceptance. Through this work, I examine the objects, emotions, and narratives that tether me to an unhealed vibration. Each object becomes a ritual of release, an offering to impermanence, a quiet act of learning to coexist with grief rather than overcome it. At its core, this series is about grief: how it lingers, how it transforms, and how we learn to carry it with us. I am drawn to the tension between holding on and letting go, the way grief and love intertwine, and how healing is not a destination but a process of continuous unraveling. In this space, I invite viewers to reflect on their own attachments and to consider what they are still carrying, and what they may finally be ready to lay to rest."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My work explores the intangible, including memory, dreams, and the shifting spaces between reality and imagination. I am drawn to fragments that linger, such as inherited stories, fleeting moments, and the blurred line between what is remembered and what is forgotten. Through photography, textiles, and sculpture, I create spaces where the unseen and the unspoken take form."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Raised on the U.S./Mexico border by Peruvian and German immigrant parents, my background informs a sense of in-betweenness that runs through my practice. Together, these mediums act as vessels for memory and as sites of transformation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My work is my way of letting you in, into the spaces between cultures, identities, and histories that shape who I am. Ultimately, it is an invitation to linger in ambiguity and to consider how memory, longing, and the intangible shape not only who we are, but how we connect with one another."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Chantal-Lesley-But-You-Don_t-Mean-A-Thing-To-Me.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Chantal Lesley, But You Don’t Mean A Thing To Me"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Epiphany Knedler: How did your project come about?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chantal Lesley: This work came out of a period of my life when, honestly, almost everything felt like it was unraveling. article_text:
Chantal Lesley: As I Lay It All To Rest

©Chantal Lesley, My Heart Grows Colder With Each Day (The Prize)

I came across Chantal Lesley’s work over this past summer. She submitted to nice;04 , the fourth annual contemporary art exhibition with Midwest Nice Art , an art collective I founded with my husband, Tim Rickett. We both really enjoyed Lesley’s submission, which was from the series Contained , and took a look at her other series. As I Lay It All To Rest really stuck with me in its ability to show the underlying feelings of grief and letting go that are difficult to name. The images are uncanny and surreal, with the hint of a dream you may have had but can’t remember. Spend some time with these images and I’m sure you’ll find something new and unexplainable too.

©Chantal Lesley, Learning To Love a Butterfly

Chantal Lesley (she/her) is an Austin-based artist, a first-generation American raised on the U.S./Mexico border, and the daughter of Peruvian and German immigrants.

Her work explores identity, memory, and belonging while increasingly engaging the intangible—dreams, the unconscious, and the shifting space between reality and imagination. Through photography, textiles, and sculpture, she creates spaces where the unseen and unspoken take form, drawing from inherited stories, fleeting moments, and the tension between remembering and forgetting. What began as an exploration of cultural identity has expanded into a broader investigation of liminality, absence, and the ways memory and longing shape how we connect to ourselves and others.

Lesley earned her BFA in Fine Art Photography from Texas State University in 2021, and her work has been shown nationally at institutions such as Houston Center for Photography, Touchstone Gallery, and Humble Arts Foundation. She has participated in residencies such as LATITUDE (Chicago, IL), Vermont Studio Center (Johnson, VT), Château d’Orquevaux (France), KUNSTRAUM (Brooklyn, NY), and Kala Art Institute (Berkeley, CA).

She is currently a member of ICOSA, an artist-run collective gallery in Austin, TX.

Follow Chantal on Instagram: @chantallesley

©Chantal Lesley, Let the Quiet Hold It

As I Lay It All To Rest

We carry so much within us: Memories, regrets, unspoken words, and lingering ghosts that echo in the quiet hours of the night. As I Lay It All to Rest is an excavation of these restless thoughts, an exploration of what it means to release, to surrender, and to live with the weight of what cannot be undone. This body of work emerges from sleepless nights and the raw space between longing and acceptance. Through this work, I examine the objects, emotions, and narratives that tether me to an unhealed vibration. Each object becomes a ritual of release, an offering to impermanence, a quiet act of learning to coexist with grief rather than overcome it. At its core, this series is about grief: how it lingers, how it transforms, and how we learn to carry it with us. I am drawn to the tension between holding on and letting go, the way grief and love intertwine, and how healing is not a destination but a process of continuous unraveling. In this space, I invite viewers to reflect on their own attachments and to consider what they are still carrying, and what they may finally be ready to lay to rest.

My work explores the intangible, including memory, dreams, and the shifting spaces between reality and imagination. I am drawn to fragments that linger, such as inherited stories, fleeting moments, and the blurred line between what is remembered and what is forgotten. Through photography, textiles, and sculpture, I create spaces where the unseen and the unspoken take form.

Raised on the U.S./Mexico border by Peruvian and German immigrant parents, my background informs a sense of in-betweenness that runs through my practice. What began as an investigation of cultural identity has evolved into a broader exploration of liminality, examining the thresholds between belonging and alienation, presence and absence, and the personal and the collective.

My process is both self-reflective and generative. Photography grounds my work in the real, while textiles weave together fragmented narratives, and sculpture gives shape to the ephemeral. Together, these mediums act as vessels for memory and as sites of transformation.

My work is my way of letting you in, into the spaces between cultures, identities, and histories that shape who I am. Ultimately, it is an invitation to linger in ambiguity and to consider how memory, longing, and the intangible shape not only who we are, but how we connect with one another.

©Chantal Lesley, But You Don’t Mean A Thing To Me

Epiphany Knedler: How did your project come about?

Chantal Lesley: This work came out of a period of my life when, honestly, almost everything felt like it was unraveling. Around 2022, a lot of different things seemed to fall apart at once, and it forced me to really confront my mental and emotional health in a way I hadn’t before.

I needed somewhere to put everything I was carrying: grief, regret, shame, memories, and all of the stories I kept replaying in my head. Eventually, making work became a way for me to process some of that.

Interestingly, I couldn’t actually make this body of work while I was in the middle of that experience. Everything was too close. I needed some distance before I could really understand what I had been feeling and figure out how to translate it into images. Once I had that distance, I was able to approach those experiences in a way that felt much calmer and more contemplative.

That distance also changed the way I thought about healing. For me, laying something to rest doesn’t mean forgetting it or reaching some perfect sense of closure. It means getting to a point where something can exist in your life without continuing to control it. The grief is still there. The memories are still there. But instead of fighting them, I can sit beside them.

I think that’s ultimately what this work is about: not closure, but coexistence.

©Chantal Lesley, Outgrowing Pains

EK: Is there a specific image that is your favorite or particularly meaningful to this series?

CL: Definitely Outgrowing Pains . I actually made that photograph in 2022, right in the middle of that chaotic period.

It’s a photograph of my own foot with a tattoo referencing Shel Silverstein’s The Giving Tree . When I was in my early 20s, I really identified with the tree and its willingness to constantly give of itself. At the time, I saw that as a positive representation of who I was. As I got into my 30s, though, I started to recognize how unhealthy that kind of boundaryless version of myself actually was.

Tattoo removal wasn’t really in my budget, so I decided to remove the tattoo photographically instead. The photograph ended up sitting on its own for a few years. Then, in 2025, when the larger concept for As I Lay It All to Rest finally clicked into place, I realized that this photograph was actually the beginning of the entire body of work.

It became the first visual articulation of a question I kept coming back to: What parts of ourselves do we have to let go of in order to become healthier versions of ourselves?

©Chantal Lesley, Between the Bloom and the Break

That’s a pretty heavy question, but I think the work allowed me to approach it gently. I like that the photographs can hold something difficult without necessarily feeling difficult to look at.

EK: Can you tell us about your artistic practice?

CL: My process is very conceptual and introspective. I would say probably 70% of the work happens in my head before I ever pick up a camera.

A lot of my ideas come from resting, journaling, having conversations, or even just noticing a word or phrase that creates a really vivid image in my mind. Language is often the bridge between what I’m feeling and what I eventually make. I’ve started thinking of myself as a visual poet because my photographs often begin with language rather than an image. Sometimes it’s a sentence, a phrase, or even a single word that suddenly turns into a whole visual in my head.

Once I have that image, I’ll usually make a rough sketch and spend some time refining the composition mentally. By the time I actually pick up the camera, I generally know what I’m trying to make. The shoot itself can happen pretty quickly because most of the work has already happened during that quiet thinking stage.

That doesn’t mean I’m rigid when I’m shooting. I always leave room for experimentation and for something unexpected to happen. But I’ve gotten much better at trusting myself and my process, and my final photographs are often surprisingly close to the images I had originally imagined.

I also think As I Lay It All to Rest represents a pretty important shift in my practice. For a long time, my work was heavily rooted in my multicultural upbringing and questions of identity. Those things are still very much a part of me, and I don’t think I’ll ever completely move away from them. But this project gave me permission to move beyond autobiography and explore more universal experiences like grief, memory, change, and emotional weight.

That shift felt vulnerable because I was moving away from something I had always considered central to my practice. But it also showed me that my own experiences don’t have to stay entirely personal. They can be a starting point for exploring something other people might recognize in themselves.

I think of my work a little like a lighthouse. I’m putting something out into the world and hoping it finds the people who need it. I don’t necessarily want to tell someone what to feel when they look at my work. I’d rather create enough space for them to bring their own experiences to it.

It took me a long time to become comfortable with the gray areas of life, of thinking, and of feeling. I used to want things to have clear answers or clear endings. Now I’m much more interested in the spaces in between. I think my work is an invitation to sit in those spaces for a little while.

©Chantal Lesley, Don’t Come Looking For Me, I Don’t Want To Be Found

EK: What’s next for you?

CL: Honestly, I’m not totally sure yet, and I’m okay with that. I don’t have a specific exhibition or project coming up that I need to announce right now. I’m in that weird in-between stage where I’m thinking a lot, journaling, collecting ideas, and trying to figure out what I want to make next.

I am in the very early stages of what I think will become a pretty long-form project with my cousin. She likes to consider herself the family archivist, and we’ve been talking a lot about our family history and the different ways our families stayed connected during the 1990s and early 2000s. We’re particularly interested in the different forms of communication they used to stay in touch across distance, and what those records might tell us about our family, migration, and the ways we maintained relationships alongside the evolution of technology.

It’s still very much in the research and collecting stage, so I don’t really know what the project will become yet. And I think that’s part of what excites me about it.

A lot of my work starts as an idea that sits in my head for a while before I know what it’s going to become. So, I guess what’s next is figuring out what’s next. And honestly, I kind of like being in that space.

©Chantal Lesley, It’s Just a Feeling

©Chantal Lesley, Nothing Grew There Anymore

©Chantal Lesley, Practicing the Art of Letting Go (Butter)

©Chantal Lesley, Tethered Dissonance

©Chantal Lesley, What’s a (Lover)Girl To Do

Epiphany Knedler is an interdisciplinary artist + educator exploring the ways we engage with history. She graduated from the University of South Dakota with a BFA in Studio Art and a BA in Political Science and completed her MFA in Studio Art at East Carolina University. She is based in Aberdeen, South Dakota, serving as an Assistant Professor of Art and Chair of the Art Department at Northern State University, a Content Editor with LENSCRATCH, and the co-founder and curator of the art collective Midwest Nice Art. Her work has been exhibited in the New York Times, the Guardian, Vermont Center for Photography, Lenscratch, Dek Unu Arts, and awarded through Lensculture, the Lucie Foundation, F-Stop Magazine, and Photolucida Critical Mass.

Follow Epiphany on Instagram: @epiphanysk

Weekly Newsletter

To Live Is to Believe

Remembering Ursula von Rydingsvard, an Epstein survivor’s message for MoMA, interviews with Paul Pfeiffer and Layli Long Soldier, and the best costumes of our artsy Halloween party.

On a fair afternoon in Queens, New York, a woman in a red dress crosses the street in front of me with an actual axe under her arm. Her face is stern, her step fast, and you can tell from the blood on her axe that she wasn’t using it to chop wood. A police siren wails in the distance, but that doesn’t seem to bother her.

I reach to lock the car and then remember it’s Halloween.

At a warm and lovely dinner at Cabinet Magazine , founder and editor-in-chief Sina Najafi shows us a photograph of tightrope walker Margret Zimmermann balancing on a high wire above the bombed-out ruins of the Haymarket in Cologne, Germany, in 1946. She looks her finest in her red lipstick, but a treacherous wind is blowing in her hair as a crowd watches from far below.

Outside, Brooklyn seems to be getting richer and poorer at the same time. A man wearing a bejeweled crown asks me for money. In this city, performance artists are beggars and beggars are performance artists.

At Hyperallergic’s art-themed Halloween party, dozens of guests show up with impressive costumes and really commit to the act. Claire Valdez, an artist and organizer who’s running for Congress, drops by and serves as a judge in our art costume contest. I don’t have a costume, but I perform all night.

“To live is to believe,” Marcel Duchamp says in a video on my phone screen. A little girl dressed as Lady Liberty crosses the street with her mother, a torch in her hand. She keeps the torch held high as they walk off, and that makes me smile.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

article_text:
Indian thespian Nawazuddin Siddiqui is attached to lead “ Kabootar ,” the debut feature from writer-director Ishan Sharma, produced by Nikhil Chaudhary of MDC Filmworks.

The film is structured as a co-production between MDC Filmworks in India, Haiku Films in France, and Rein Film in Norway, with Rohit Saxena serving as co-producer on the Indian side. Principal photography is scheduled to begin in Delhi in early 2027.

Bravo Renews 'In the City, 'Next Gen NYC' and 'Southern Hospitality,' Orders 'Next Gen Atlanta' and Craig Conover-Led Microdrama 'Charmed by a Southern Monster'

Set against the crumbling architecture of Old Delhi, “Kabootar” centers on Mehboob, a street detective who secretly reads letters written to a Djinn in search of prospective clients. His path crosses with Naoko, a Japanese tourist carrying the weight of a painful past, and Ruby, a young child searching for his parents.

Popular on Variety

Siddiqui is among the most decorated actors of his generation in Indian cinema. He has appeared in Anurag Kashyap’s “Gangs of Wasseypur,” Ritesh Batra’s “The Lunchbox,” and Nandita Das’s “Manto” – all of which debuted in Cannes – and starred in Netflix’s hit thriller series “Sacred Games.” He received an International Emmy nomination for his lead role in Netflix film “Serious Men.”

Chaudhary said: “Nawaz is an actor of extraordinary range. He can be dangerous in ‘Gangs of Wasseypur’ and heartbreakingly gentle in ‘The Lunchbox.’ He’s also one of the few Indian actors with a real international presence. His films have gone to Cannes multiple times, and he has been nominated for an International Emmy. For an India-France-Norway co-production, that matters enormously in taking ‘Kabootar’ to audiences around the world. Just as important, he knows Delhi intimately. For Ishan and I, this film is a love letter to the city, and we needed an actor who could understand it, feel it and embody it. He does all three.”

Sharma, who developed the script through the production and storytelling Workshop at the Festival des 3 Continents in Nantes – formerly known as the Produire au Sud Workshop – added: “Nawaz has been an invisible collaborator to a generation of young writers and directors, myself included. We write with his performances in our minds. From ‘Anwar Ka Ajab Kissa’ to ‘The Lunchbox,’ I’ve always admired the intensity and love he brings to a character, and his rare ability to move between hope and despair, light and dark, without losing either. ‘Kabootar’ asks something of him that audiences haven’t seen before. To have him take that leap with us is a gift. I can’t wait to build this world with him.”

The project has been selected for a series of international market showcases, including the Tasveer Film Market in Seattle, Film Bazaar in Goa – organized by India’s National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) – and the NFDC lineup at this year’s European Film Market in Berlin. Later this month, Chaudhary will pitch the film in the APN+ Track of the Asian Producers Network in Singapore.

Casting director Dilip Shankar, whose credits include “Life of Pi” and “Monsoon Wedding,” said: “Nawazuddin will bring Mehboob’s eccentric humor, emotional depth and quiet vulnerability to life with rare authenticity. The character demands mischief, rage, tenderness and grace. With his rooted presence and remarkable nuance, Nawazuddin embodies Mehboob’s essential contradictions. His performance anchors ‘Kabootar’ in the lived-in, poignant texture of Old Delhi.”

Sharma is a graduate of the Satyajit Ray Film & Television Institute. His short films “The God of Panic Street” (2019) and “A Season of Mangoes” (2022) have played international festivals and collected several awards, including the Cinema Experimenta Award.

MDC Filmworks has previously produced five films, among them Sanjoy Nag’s “Yours Truly,” which premiered at the Busan International Film Festival, and Rajat Kapoor’s dark comedy “Kadakh,” which premiered at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, where it won best screenplay. Haiku Films, founded by Thomas Jaeger, Antoine Delahousse, and Claire Trinquet, produced “Fi” (Grand Prize, San Sebastián 2022) and co-produced “Treasure” (Berlinale 2024). Rein Film, founded by Mathis Ståle Mathisen and Aleksander Olai Korsnes, is known for “My Fathers’ Daughter” (Toronto 2024).

Key crew includes cinematographer Udit Khurana (“Bayaan,” “Ghaath”), sound designer Sethu Venugopal (“Mother,” “Nocturnal Burger”), and casting director Shankar.

“Kabootar” was curated by CineV, Nina Lath Gupta’s platform connecting projects with financiers and investors.

title_original: 從熱天午後的混沌之地，走進紫羅蘭的凌波夢境──與康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼談，一個語言之外的世界
title_zh: 從熱天午後的混沌之地，走進紫羅蘭的凌波夢境──與康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼談，一個語言之外的世界
summary_zh: 来源摘录：在柯薩瑪尼的電影語言之前，我們或許可以將她的電影旅程，視為「追尋」本身。那是向下連結前世、向上連結靈魂本質的靈薄獄，而意識之於靈薄獄的凌波追尋，我們可能稱之為「夢境」。透過在夢境世界裡的追尋，柯薩瑪尼看見的「赤子之心」並非全然的潔淨、良善，而是走進一個不一定需要意義，於是能擁有萬千意義的流轉世界。 這篇文章 從熱天午後的混沌之地，走進紫羅蘭的凌波夢境──與康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼談，一個語言之外的世界 最早出現於 釀電影 。

Mary Didn't Know）。", "links": [{"text": "2026 高雄電影節", "url": "https://filmaholic.tw/covers/2026kff/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "早於 2014 年，柯薩瑪尼便以《雅典熱天午後》獲得該屆高雄電影節「國際短片競賽」單元之優選，2016 年再以《混沌之子》獲同單元之奇幻火球獎，若要系譜性地理解柯薩瑪尼電影裡的詩意，那麼按出品年份觀看其作，或許便能從中窺見電影象徵的連結和留白。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "這樣的聯繫，同時也影響著觀眾如何看待電影，以及電影裡的寫實世界，與自身所處的真實世界之間的共鳴。在觀看柯薩瑪尼電影時，若要還原電影與真實世界的連結，多半只能從文字化的電影介紹知悉一二。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "比如，首作《雅典熱天午後》靈感起於 2004 年雅典奧運，外來棕櫚樹帶來啃食樹心的紅象鼻蟲，最終僅剩為數不多的、樹心乾癟、細小的品種能夠存活；延續《雅典熱天午後》的《黃塵樹語》，則追溯看似更為古老的故事，每一棵棕櫚樹都代表著一個患病的家庭，熱天城市籠罩黃色粉塵，眼望城市各處，不見人煙只見樹影。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，影中人仍戮力追求言語的方式。我們想要聆聽長頸鹿心臟的搏動，以此通曉自然萬物密隱的連結，我們想要明瞭樹的語言，在覆滅之中願望野長的新生。電影裡的非語言，實際上更接近人如何學會語言。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "學會一種嶄新的語言，是追尋意在言外的情感，只不過回到人類之間的語言，就像柯薩瑪尼電影裡出現過西班牙語、瑞典語、柏柏爾語、塞爾維亞語，依賴著翻譯字幕的我們，卻也可能在聆聽中，將之視為同一種語言，於是既無法通達心靈內面的感受，更難以理解多種語言背後所牽涉的希臘群島族群、歷史問題。"}, {"type": "image", "url": 提及柯薩瑪尼系列電影的內在精神，她自承一切起因於成長過程所經驗的多種語言，以及語言背後的文化差異。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在巴別塔之後的語言，其存在目的不再只是為了溝通，也包含尋找語言中的「盲點」。 面對著多元的語言、文化，與其背後複雜的政治成因，之於柯薩瑪尼歷來作品的連結，她先是以仍在發展中的劇本解釋道。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "還在劇本階段的新電影，描述一名中國女人移民至希臘，在購置房產時因語言、文化差異而起的一連串誤會。近十年的希臘移民政策，有大批中國人因政治、疫病等原因，舉家搬遷、移民至希臘；在希臘持「黃金簽證」的人口中，有近半數為中國人，其中更有超過 70% 人口，最終獲得永久居留卡。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "「這部新電影的敘事核心是『誤譯』，筆下的角色與生活在現實世界的我們，是有些重疊的，但也可能因為敘事角度不同，而創造出全然不同的敘事。中國人會將 Aegeus 稱之為『愛琴海』，而希臘人總會將『愛琴海』唸成『哀琴海』，無論是移民或原本住民，生活在 Aegeus 周遭的生活，都可能因為彼此的遷徙、移居，帶來愛或哀愁。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因為口音而致的有趣誤會，當然是柯薩瑪尼自身浮想聯翩的連結，但是她想更進一步地思考「語言」的誤譯， 「我的創作經常源自我的『奇想』（Fantasy），在探索語言之間的差異、誤譯時，我們總能從中窺見人類內心的世界，因為語言關於對不同文化的想像、詮釋，以及個體在一段生活、一段情感的記憶，而那些我感到興趣的事物，都是語言表達之外的，藏在心靈世界的綺想。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在不同的詮釋版本中，有一說為希臘建城英雄忒修斯（Thēseus）在進入前往半人半牛米諾陶洛斯（Minotaurus）的迷宮之前，其父埃勾斯（Aegeus）與之約定，若是平安歸來便要掛上純白色的船帆。最終，忒修斯歸來時因故未換上白色船帆，埃勾斯誤以為兒子已死，便絕望地投海自盡，於是群島之間的海域才以 Aegeus 為名。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "柯薩瑪尼從源於生活的細小差異，嘗試看見不同的敘事，她認為「語言」的真意，其實是在通天的巴別塔之前，拼湊出關於萬物共通情感的地圖， 「這是藝術家的工作，我們一直在挖掘人類當前景況、內心世界與情感根源的交集，在彼此交疊的圓心之中，我想那就是關於溝通的全新途徑。」"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://img.vocus.cc/60MPwxnDgj2P0AeU9DgjucmlFpfOVotTvCTBmQnBnEM/w:740/f:jpg/plain/https://images.vocus.cc/933ab080-72bb-4005-8af1-a8e23c9b76cb.jpg", "alt": "2026 高雄電影節「焦點影人」，導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina "https://img.vocus.cc/uaTXpABUFECRJZ_PT9RdcI-Y8LgFpghdOI-A50hlZF8/w:740/f:jpg/plain/https://images.vocus.cc/4164d33f-e908-47c7-8f23-605d99fae1cd.jpg", "alt": "《混沌之子》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節", "caption": "", "credit": "釀電影"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《混沌之子》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在柯薩瑪尼的電影語言之前，我們或許可以將她的電影旅程，視為「追尋」本身。那是處在冥河之外、審判席之前，向下連結前世、向上連結靈魂本質的靈薄獄（Limbo），而意識之於靈薄獄的凌波追尋，我們可能將之稱為「夢境」。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "夢境，當然關於生命的歷史。追溯至希臘神話的靈薄獄象徵，是黑帝斯（Hades）的地下世界，被稱為「水仙平野」（Asphodel Meadows）的亡靈居所；荷馬史詩提及水仙平野猶如蒼白、恍惚的夢境世界，亡靈上不了至福，卻也不致落入地獄深處。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中有著戰爭時作壁上觀、無有行動的天使，也有未受洗便早夭的孩童靈魂，而在但丁的敘述中，亡靈之處是深切嘆息所組成的陰翳大地。但是，我們要如何看待源於柯薩瑪尼自身的夢境，卻也興發自真實世界的《雅典熱天午後》和《黃塵樹語》？ 它畢竟與真實世界息息相關，同樣指認出資本主義、經濟危機下的都市末日，更能將之視為對未來世界的寓言，難道在柯薩瑪尼電影裡的眾人，皆是《混沌之子》裡純真得邪惡、邪惡得純真的赤子嗎？"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "取自傳頌千年的神話，柯薩瑪尼結合自身的信仰經驗，創造出混淆傳說與夢境的精神世界。因此，她的電影世界，也更像是夢境世界的延伸，以此指認出寫實世界之外的語言， 「在我很小的時候，我的奶奶加入基督教派的新興宗教，她的教會相信世界終將會變成『天堂』，人類最終會和所有動物和睦共處，與奶奶一起研讀聖經所帶來的影響，也體現在我早期的創作中，人類和動物、植物就像處身在另一個世界。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "透過在夢境世界裡的追尋，柯薩瑪尼看見的「赤子之心」並非全然的潔淨、良善，而是在歲時祓除人類社會行禮如儀的教條之後，走進一個不一定需要意義，於是能擁有萬千意義的流轉世界。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://img.vocus.cc/EOhpuRZbgSZ3dBPEZD_hbfodzkbygUvWtnerkvFHYu8/w:740/f:jpg/plain/https://images.vocus.cc/bfefd620-df34-43c2-bdbe-b757f77ce370.jpg", "alt": "2026 高雄電影節「焦點影人」，導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina "https://img.vocus.cc/CCRgK3RXbZy9zvpnr5U9T3mfcngp2i9Q50RpBzzs6xY/w:740/f:jpg/plain/https://images.vocus.cc/0ea8c410-4c19-4423-a3fa-451675fd8860.jpg", "alt": "《混沌之子》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節", "caption": "", "《混沌之子》被焚毀的聖母像，與尋找鯨魚的一群孩子，帶來荒涼卻哀艷的寓意，我們的確能將其中的追尋，以白化症男孩出現前後的人物、鏡頭調度相互對照，於是後設地意識到導演目光的所在，以及其與當前世界的連結。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "若是要將《混沌之子》視為柯薩瑪尼的創作轉折，也興許能更為清晰地，指出父權社會對年幼男性的宰制，或者進步主義下遭邊緣化的其他思想；然而，正因為柯薩瑪尼將世界視為「混沌」本身，因此過分清楚的指涉，都可能反過來模糊了其中的觀看之道。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "即使柯薩瑪尼的創作核心，依然抱持極高的人文精神，且她所關注的事物也與真實世界緊密相連，但是關於男孩、鯨魚的象徵之意，便是在我們意識到創作目光的「不在」之後，才能提煉出其中的詩意。"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "「我並不會說，我的電影是『象徵性』的，我只是在既有的現實之上，利用奇幻元素去創造另一層現實。在我的所有電影中，每一個元素都有自己的主體性，有自己的存在與感受，這才是情感本質的真實。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而面對敘事邏輯難以銜接的問題，柯薩瑪尼則認為觀眾仍能透過感官的（Sensorial）體驗來經驗電影。 「我認為這樣的體驗才是屬於人類本質的歷程：我們如何不只是理解世界的外在、連結外在與真實，而是真正體察在事物內面的、心靈內在的感受。」"}, {"type": "image", "url": "作為藝術家的理解，《混沌之子》代表著柯薩瑪尼創作的核心精神，包含刻劃基督教社會背後的父權色彩，而片中的「鯨魚」之意則是她創造路上的陰性實踐，且不只是連結古老傳說，更旨在翻轉神話的陳舊寓意。"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "「我認為《混沌之子》所具備的能量，就像是那頭沙灘上的巨鯨，我們很難分清牠是活物、死物，牠龐大得令人畏懼，卻美麗得令人驚艷，牠既與『災難』相連，卻又與『生命』緊密連結。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《混沌之子》一段，引述《以賽亞書》11 章 6 節（Isaiah 11：6）：「豺狼必與羊羔同居，豹子與山羊羔同臥；少壯獅子與牛犢並肥畜同群；小孩子要牽引牠們。」（The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid；and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.）"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，柯薩瑪尼的理解，並非神的恩澤將灌溉世界，她只是揣想著，猛獸、犢羊與人類，皆蘊含著自己的生命力量， 若是將萬物的生命精神匯聚成一個灰色的世界，那就像我們看見一頭擱淺的巨鯨，與之對望所帶來的撼動，也僅僅只是一個生命看見了另一個生命的存在，如此而已。"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "「總有人會提到，我的電影有一種冷冽、疏離的特質，但我不是要逃避情感，我只是想用常人所不習慣的方式，來觀察、實驗『情感』的歸處在何方。所謂的『現實』──我們活著的『現實』，它究竟是什麼？在現實世界裡，不存在絕對的真理，我認為『情感中的真實』是更重要的。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "回到柯薩瑪尼對自身創作的定義──奇想，Fantasy，詞源來自希臘語「phantastikós」，字根動詞「phainō」具有「將內在的事物顯露於外在」之意。 柯薩瑪尼認為，她的電影便是不斷地翻找生命、心靈內面難以表達的事物，並嘗試以影像表達其徵狀、情感，一如生命之所以復興，便是源於對「死亡」的目標。"}, {"type": "image", "url": 在夢境世界裡，場景本如記憶般跳接呈現，看見一片金黃色澤的汪洋，可能讓我們想起童年記憶裡，曾經路過的發光柏油路，卻想不起來那一條路為何而走，又將前往何方。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但是那一片汪洋，也可能讓我們想起兒時端著一杯滿溢的水，因為晃動而來回潑灑，水波之間泛起的午後光澤。 事件與事件之間，關係與關係之間，就像是記憶──或者說是機運──所賦予的隨機群戲，連串的記憶就像陌生人共同組成的一座大廈、一艘郵輪，在事物被命運串起之前，我們都難以察覺其中的指引。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "從《電幻天鵝》裡，老邁但是富裕的寡婦，跳著芭蕾的少女，發了貧窮惡夢的女孩；到《人魚戀習曲》閃動金光色與紫羅蘭的人魚女孩，柯薩瑪尼在看見名古屋人魚學校的照片時，轉瞬想起童年經常做的巨浪惡夢。"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "「那是一個關於巨浪的惡夢，小時候我經常夢見自己被巨浪所吞噬，有時甚至會不敢入睡，深怕自己醒來時，會發現自己真的處身在汪洋之中。後來，我在一次的催眠治療中，理解了我的前世是一名死於巨浪的日本女人。撰寫《人魚戀習曲》的劇本時，我又不斷地夢見巨浪的夢，然而面對惡夢、面對巨浪的恐懼，就像是過往的女性所受到的痛苦，如今它在我身上降臨，是為了讓我療癒這份哀慟。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "隨著深入研究人魚學校，也實際到日本走訪、進行拍攝，柯薩瑪尼發覺自己必須將源於生命深層的恐懼，與當前的女性議題彼此呼應，才能回返屬於生命的古老記憶，進而連結「日本女人」的「前世」。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "在日本，紫色是屬於嫉妒的顏色，混合了藍色與紅色的紫色，也帶有酷兒的氣質；在希臘則有詩人莎芙（Sappho）寫道，母親在年輕時，紫色髮帶將是最好的裝飾物，而髮色比火焰還黃的女孩，則適合戴上綻放花朵所編織的花圈。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "為紫羅蘭所覆蓋的雅典古城，亞里斯多德（Aristotélēs）認為海浪揚起金光色的陰影時，海洋便帶著紫色的氣息，因此在陰翳中反而明亮的紫羅蘭色，紫色的少女既是前世也是今生，指認危機卻也帶來嶄新。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《人魚戀習曲》的紫羅蘭人魚女孩，在真實世界是柯薩瑪尼的女性主義實踐，在傳說世界則是對海妖傳說的顛覆，面對現實和夢境的恐懼，透過拍電影所帶來的體驗而得到了轉化。"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "「尤其是在女孩透過歌唱成為賽蓮（Siren）的那一刻，她同時也成為了那頭巨大的鯨魚、那道巨大的海浪，危險卻也迷人，而在我們大聲歌唱的時候，也代表生命不會只有當一個邪惡的女巫，或者當一個順從的妻子、母親，我們可以同時擁有這兩種選擇，世界也應該接受這樣的我們。」"}, {"type": "image", "url": article_text:
採訪、撰文／黃曦 專訪攝影／ioauue 劇照提供／高雄電影節 責任編輯／黃曦 核稿編輯／黃曦

2026 高雄電影節 「焦點影人」為希臘導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina Kotzamani），除了柯薩瑪尼的最新作品、首部劇情長片《人魚戀習曲》（Titanic Ocean，2026），也選映歷來的五部劇情短片作品：2014 年《雅典熱天午後》（Washingtonia）、2015 年《黃塵樹語》（Yellow Fieber）、2016 年《混沌之子》（Limbo）、2019 年《電幻天鵝》（Electric Swan）、2024 年《瑪麗不知道的事》（What Mary Didn't Know）。

早於 2014 年，柯薩瑪尼便以《雅典熱天午後》獲得該屆高雄電影節「國際短片競賽」單元之優選，2016 年再以《混沌之子》獲同單元之奇幻火球獎，若要系譜性地理解柯薩瑪尼電影裡的詩意，那麼按出品年份觀看其作，或許便能從中窺見電影象徵的連結和留白。

那些在柯薩瑪尼電影裡，看似無以連貫、或是未曾謝幕的情節，其實源自與現實之間的扞格與斷裂。首先是關於語言的，柯薩瑪尼經常透過非語言的方式，建立起人類與動物、植物，甚至是無形存在之間的聯繫。

2026 高雄電影節「焦點影人」，導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina Kotzamani）專訪。／專訪攝影：ioauue

這樣的聯繫，同時也影響著觀眾如何看待電影，以及電影裡的寫實世界，與自身所處的真實世界之間的共鳴。在觀看柯薩瑪尼電影時，若要還原電影與真實世界的連結，多半只能從文字化的電影介紹知悉一二。

比如，首作《雅典熱天午後》靈感起於 2004 年雅典奧運，外來棕櫚樹帶來啃食樹心的紅象鼻蟲，最終僅剩為數不多的、樹心乾癟、細小的品種能夠存活；延續《雅典熱天午後》的《黃塵樹語》，則追溯看似更為古老的故事，每一棵棕櫚樹都代表著一個患病的家庭，熱天城市籠罩黃色粉塵，眼望城市各處，不見人煙只見樹影。

然而，影中人仍戮力追求言語的方式。我們想要聆聽長頸鹿心臟的搏動，以此通曉自然萬物密隱的連結，我們想要明瞭樹的語言，在覆滅之中願望野長的新生。電影裡的非語言，實際上更接近人如何學會語言。

學會一種嶄新的語言，是追尋意在言外的情感，只不過回到人類之間的語言，就像柯薩瑪尼電影裡出現過西班牙語、瑞典語、柏柏爾語、塞爾維亞語，依賴著翻譯字幕的我們，卻也可能在聆聽中，將之視為同一種語言，於是既無法通達心靈內面的感受，更難以理解多種語言背後所牽涉的希臘群島族群、歷史問題。

《雅典熱天午後》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

《雅典熱天午後》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

為了理解柯薩瑪尼電影最外在的形式，我們必須先從表現其敘事的外在談起，才可能觸及其中不可見、卻又建基在世界底部的共通性，也就是語言所呈示的文化脈絡。 提及柯薩瑪尼系列電影的內在精神，她自承一切起因於成長過程所經驗的多種語言，以及語言背後的文化差異。

在巴別塔之後的語言，其存在目的不再只是為了溝通，也包含尋找語言中的「盲點」。 面對著多元的語言、文化，與其背後複雜的政治成因，之於柯薩瑪尼歷來作品的連結，她先是以仍在發展中的劇本解釋道。

還在劇本階段的新電影，描述一名中國女人移民至希臘，在購置房產時因語言、文化差異而起的一連串誤會。近十年的希臘移民政策，有大批中國人因政治、疫病等原因，舉家搬遷、移民至希臘；在希臘持「黃金簽證」的人口中，有近半數為中國人，其中更有超過 70% 人口，最終獲得永久居留卡。

2026 高雄電影節「焦點影人」，導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina Kotzamani）專訪。／專訪攝影：ioauue

「這部新電影的敘事核心是『誤譯』，筆下的角色與生活在現實世界的我們，是有些重疊的，但也可能因為敘事角度不同，而創造出全然不同的敘事。中國人會將 Aegeus 稱之為『愛琴海』，而希臘人總會將『愛琴海』唸成『哀琴海』，無論是移民或原本住民，生活在 Aegeus 周遭的生活，都可能因為彼此的遷徙、移居，帶來愛或哀愁。」

因為口音而致的有趣誤會，當然是柯薩瑪尼自身浮想聯翩的連結，但是她想更進一步地思考「語言」的誤譯， 「我的創作經常源自我的『奇想』（Fantasy），在探索語言之間的差異、誤譯時，我們總能從中窺見人類內心的世界，因為語言關於對不同文化的想像、詮釋，以及個體在一段生活、一段情感的記憶，而那些我感到興趣的事物，都是語言表達之外的，藏在心靈世界的綺想。」

在不同的詮釋版本中，有一說為希臘建城英雄忒修斯（Thēseus）在進入前往半人半牛米諾陶洛斯（Minotaurus）的迷宮之前，其父埃勾斯（Aegeus）與之約定，若是平安歸來便要掛上純白色的船帆。最終，忒修斯歸來時因故未換上白色船帆，埃勾斯誤以為兒子已死，便絕望地投海自盡，於是群島之間的海域才以 Aegeus 為名。

柯薩瑪尼從源於生活的細小差異，嘗試看見不同的敘事，她認為「語言」的真意，其實是在通天的巴別塔之前，拼湊出關於萬物共通情感的地圖， 「這是藝術家的工作，我們一直在挖掘人類當前景況、內心世界與情感根源的交集，在彼此交疊的圓心之中，我想那就是關於溝通的全新途徑。」

2026 高雄電影節「焦點影人」，導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina Kotzamani）專訪。／專訪攝影：ioauue

《混沌之子》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

在柯薩瑪尼的電影語言之前，我們或許可以將她的電影旅程，視為「追尋」本身。那是處在冥河之外、審判席之前，向下連結前世、向上連結靈魂本質的靈薄獄（Limbo），而意識之於靈薄獄的凌波追尋，我們可能將之稱為「夢境」。

夢境，當然關於生命的歷史。追溯至希臘神話的靈薄獄象徵，是黑帝斯（Hades）的地下世界，被稱為「水仙平野」（Asphodel Meadows）的亡靈居所；荷馬史詩提及水仙平野猶如蒼白、恍惚的夢境世界，亡靈上不了至福，卻也不致落入地獄深處。

其中有著戰爭時作壁上觀、無有行動的天使，也有未受洗便早夭的孩童靈魂，而在但丁的敘述中，亡靈之處是深切嘆息所組成的陰翳大地。但是，我們要如何看待源於柯薩瑪尼自身的夢境，卻也興發自真實世界的《雅典熱天午後》和《黃塵樹語》？ 它畢竟與真實世界息息相關，同樣指認出資本主義、經濟危機下的都市末日，更能將之視為對未來世界的寓言，難道在柯薩瑪尼電影裡的眾人，皆是《混沌之子》裡純真得邪惡、邪惡得純真的赤子嗎？

取自傳頌千年的神話，柯薩瑪尼結合自身的信仰經驗，創造出混淆傳說與夢境的精神世界。因此，她的電影世界，也更像是夢境世界的延伸，以此指認出寫實世界之外的語言， 「在我很小的時候，我的奶奶加入基督教派的新興宗教，她的教會相信世界終將會變成『天堂』，人類最終會和所有動物和睦共處，與奶奶一起研讀聖經所帶來的影響，也體現在我早期的創作中，人類和動物、植物就像處身在另一個世界。」

透過在夢境世界裡的追尋，柯薩瑪尼看見的「赤子之心」並非全然的潔淨、良善，而是在歲時祓除人類社會行禮如儀的教條之後，走進一個不一定需要意義，於是能擁有萬千意義的流轉世界。

《混沌之子》被焚毀的聖母像，與尋找鯨魚的一群孩子，帶來荒涼卻哀艷的寓意，我們的確能將其中的追尋，以白化症男孩出現前後的人物、鏡頭調度相互對照，於是後設地意識到導演目光的所在，以及其與當前世界的連結。

若是要將《混沌之子》視為柯薩瑪尼的創作轉折，也興許能更為清晰地，指出父權社會對年幼男性的宰制，或者進步主義下遭邊緣化的其他思想；然而，正因為柯薩瑪尼將世界視為「混沌」本身，因此過分清楚的指涉，都可能反過來模糊了其中的觀看之道。

即使柯薩瑪尼的創作核心，依然抱持極高的人文精神，且她所關注的事物也與真實世界緊密相連，但是關於男孩、鯨魚的象徵之意，便是在我們意識到創作目光的「不在」之後，才能提煉出其中的詩意。

「我並不會說，我的電影是『象徵性』的，我只是在既有的現實之上，利用奇幻元素去創造另一層現實。在我的所有電影中，每一個元素都有自己的主體性，有自己的存在與感受，這才是情感本質的真實。」

而面對敘事邏輯難以銜接的問題，柯薩瑪尼則認為觀眾仍能透過感官的（Sensorial）體驗來經驗電影。 「我認為這樣的體驗才是屬於人類本質的歷程：我們如何不只是理解世界的外在、連結外在與真實，而是真正體察在事物內面的、心靈內在的感受。」
